opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started out of curiosity more than any grand plan. When I was studying, I was doing a lot of math and computer science, and I kept hearing from friends and classmates about quant firms: how they used rigorous modeling, statistics, and heavy engineering to make decisions in really noisy, fast-moving environments. That combination really appealed to me. It felt like a place where theory actually meets reality, and you get very direct feedback on whether your ideas work.

I also wanted to understand how a different industry thinks about problems. In academia you can spend a long time on one question, and the measure of success is sometimes a bit abstract. In quant finance, the loop is much tighter. You build a model, you test it, and the data tells you pretty quickly whether you're right. I thought experiencing that kind of discipline, being careful about overfitting, thinking hard about evaluation, caring about efficiency and latency, would make me a better researcher and engineer no matter where I ended up.

So I saw it as a chance to stretch myself and learn how people solve hard problems under real constraints. A lot of what I picked up there, like the emphasis on systems performance and on measuring things carefully, ended up being really useful later when I went deeper into machine learning systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes curiosity and a desire to stretch himself, but does not say he wanted to avoid wondering about quantitative finance later.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that dealing with money every day lacked meaning; it presents quant finance as appealing for its modeling, feedback, and real-world constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started out of curiosity more than any grand plan. When I was doing my PhD, most of my work was on systems and compilers, and I kept hearing about quant firms as this place where people were pushing performance to its absolute limits. Latency measured in microseconds, every cache line mattering, the whole thing running on real markets with real money on the line. That was fascinating to me as a systems person, because it's one of the few environments where the engineering constraints are that unforgiving and the feedback is that immediate.

So I did an internship, partly to test myself. I wanted to know what it felt like to work where correctness and speed were not just research metrics but things that directly decided whether you made or lost money that day. And I learned a lot. The engineering culture was very rigorous, very pragmatic. People didn't care about elegance for its own sake. They cared about whether it worked and whether it was fast.

But I also realized something about myself during that time. The problems were hard, but they were narrow, and the results stayed inside the firm. I found I really missed the open-source side of research, where you build something and anyone in the world can pick it up and use it. That contrast actually clarified a lot for me. It's part of why I came back to building infrastructure for machine learning, where the performance problems are just as demanding, but the impact is much more public and much more shared.

r001.rationale: The response says he was curious and wanted to test himself, but does not say he chose quant finance to avoid wondering about it later.

r002.rationale: He says the work’s results stayed inside the firm and that he missed open-source research; he does not say dealing with money every day lacked meaning.
